@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — White-Glove Delivery Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The process chain for a white-glove delivery, as published on the service's hub page. Step 1, name the pieces: the client names the pieces, and each piece is assessed on its own — weight, fragile points, finish and value at risk. Step 2, match the protection: padded blankets and clear stretch wrap as the standard, a custom crate built around the piece when it needs more; high-mass pieces are surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol before they move. Step 3, receive and stage: freight arriving through the freight chain is unloaded on the warehouse floor, counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, and staged for the delivery — deconsolidated or cross-docked where a shipment needs to split or change vehicles, and reworked where needed. Step 4, deliver in on a planned route: the item crosses the threshold — never left at a curb — to homes, offices, industrial sites and retail. Step 5, place: the item is set in its final position, where it belongs. Step 6, remove packaging: the delivered item's packaging is removed, so the recipient is not left with the wrap and the boxes. Step 7, verify: placement and condition are verified with the recipient before the crew leaves. Domain reference (the general delivered-in sequence, labeled as such): appointment scheduling with the recipient and a pre-delivery access check — doorways, stairs, elevators — belong to the same chain in the industry's general practice; the company's published chain above is the company's own, and its deliveries are arranged by appointment, set when the job is scoped and quoted.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — White-Glove Delivery Levels: Domain Reference Dataset
@graph.description: Domain reference — the delivery-level ladder the industry sells, labeled as domain vocabulary, and this company's published position on it. The level describes one thing: how far the crew carries the item. Curbside: the item is left at the curb or driveway. Threshold: the item is carried inside the first door, garage or lobby, no further. Room of choice: the item is carried to the room the recipient picks; unpacking is not included. Room of choice with packaging removal: placement in the room, and the packaging is taken away. White glove: room of choice plus unpacking, inspection with the recipient, and packaging and debris removal — brought in on a planned route, set in its final position, and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves. Some providers stack assembly or installation above white glove. The names are not standardized anywhere in the industry — no regulator defines them — so two quotes can both say white glove and deliver different rooms, different unpacking and different debris outcomes; the details confirmed in writing are worth more than the level named on a quote. The company's published position: The Flat Rate Movers publishes the top of the ladder as this service's standard — placed, unpacked and verified, never a curbside drop — and publishes no lower tier as this service's offer. Assembly and installation are named here as domain tier components; in this company's published white-glove scope both are included — full assembly, with appliance hookups where the job includes appliances.

hasPart.name: On an interstate move, full value protection is the federal default
hasPart.description: Federal rules give interstate household-goods customers two liability levels. Full Value Protection is the default: if an article is lost, destroyed, or damaged in the mover's custody, the mover must repair it, replace it with one of like kind, or pay its current market replacement value. Released Value — 60 cents per pound per article — applies only when the customer signs a specific statement choosing it on the bill of lading.

citation.name: Before Requesting Services from Any Mover (Subpart B) — FMCSA Protect Your Move

additionalProperty.name: detail
additionalProperty.value: The two levels are set by 49 CFR 375.701 (released value) and 375.703 (full value). For a high-value, low-weight piece — exactly the white-glove profile — the released-value formula returns almost nothing: the protection decision belongs in writing before the move, not after a claim.

additionalProperty.name: scope
additionalProperty.value: Interstate household-goods moves under FMCSA jurisdiction; intrastate moves follow state law.

hasPart.name: Items worth more than $100 per pound must be listed in writing
hasPart.description: Under the federal full-value rules, an article of extraordinary value is any item worth more than $100 per pound — jewelry, silverware, china, furs, antiques, and artwork are the FMCSA's own examples. A mover may limit its liability for such an article unless the customer specifically lists it on the shipping documents.

citation.name: Before Requesting Services from Any Mover (Subpart B) — FMCSA Protect Your Move

additionalProperty.name: detail
additionalProperty.value: This is why a white-glove delivery starts with an item list, not a truck: the pieces that most need the careful service are the same pieces the paperwork must name individually, with their values, before custody changes hands.

hasPart.name: Valuation is not insurance — FMCSA says so in those words
hasPart.description: Valuation is the tariff-based level of carrier liability written into the moving contract; it is not an insurance policy and is not governed by state insurance law. FMCSA's consumer booklet states it directly: valuation is simply a tariff-based level of motor carrier liability.

citation.name: Frequently Asked Questions — FMCSA (liability and valuation)

additionalProperty.name: detail
additionalProperty.value: The distinction decides who pays and how much after damage: a valuation claim runs against the carrier under the contract's liability level, while third-party insurance follows its own policy terms. Both can be in play on one delivery; they are never the same instrument.

additionalProperty.name: scope

hasPart.name: The 51-pound constant is why heavy pieces move with two people
hasPart.description: NIOSH's lifting equation sets a load constant of 51 pounds under ideal conditions — the recommended weight limit is then reduced by posture, reach, frequency, and coupling multipliers. A piece above that constant, or bulky enough to wreck the multipliers, is a two-person carry as a matter of ergonomics, not preference.

citation.name: Applications Manual for the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation (Publication No. 94-110)

publisher.name: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health

@graph.name: White-Glove Delivery — The Process, Step by Step
@graph.description: The eight-step white-glove delivery process as data: item list and survey; receiving and the inspection report; the storage hold; install-day scheduling; protected transport; room-of-choice placement; unpacking, full assembly and hookups; and the close — haul-away, debris out, and the three-stage photo record delivered to the account. The same sequence the service page states in prose.

step.name: Item list and survey
step.text: The job starts as an item list — each piece named, with dimensions, weight where known, and the rooms they are bound for. The path is surveyed with it: stairs, turns, doorways, floor surfaces. High-value pieces are listed individually, with declared values, the way the federal paperwork will want them.

step.name: Receiving, inspection, and hold (account freight)
step.text: When a brand, retailer, or designer ships pieces ahead, the company receives them, inspects each piece on arrival, issues the receiving inspection report, photographs condition, and holds the pieces in storage until the install day. Freight damage is documented while the carrier can still answer for it.

step.name: Level chosen in writing
step.text: The delivery level is chosen per job and written into the flat-rate quote before work begins: white glove in full, or a lower level where the piece honestly allows it. The quote states what the level includes, so the appointment holds no surprises.

step.name: Appointment window
step.text: The delivery runs to a scheduled appointment window, arranged around the customer, the building, or the designer's install day — not an all-day wait at the curb.

step.name: Protected carry-in
step.text: Floors and doorways on the path are protected before the first piece moves. Crew size follows the piece and the path from the survey — heavy or bulky pieces travel with two people, on the NIOSH arithmetic, never on hope.

step.name: Room-of-choice placement
step.text: Each piece goes to the room the customer names and is positioned to the plan — the customer's, or the designer's instructions where a designer is running the install.

step.name: Unpack, full assembly, joint inspection
step.text: Pieces are unpacked in the room and fully assembled — the complete build the piece needs to stand and function, with appliance hookups completed where the job includes appliances. Each piece is inspected together with the customer, and condition is noted on the delivery record while both parties are looking at the item.

step.name: Packaging out, sign-off
step.text: Every piece of packaging and debris leaves with the crew. The delivery record is signed against the item list, and the room is left finished — furniture standing, nothing to break down, nothing to haul.
